introduction-the-computer-inside-your-co.core: A GPU is a separate computer on a PCIe card with thousands of simple cores, its own high-bandwidth memory (HBM or GDDR), firmware and schedulers. The CPU doesn't run GPU code directly. Through drivers it copies data to GPU memory, submits command buffers (kernels), and waits for completion. Performance and failures depend on that relationship: PCIe bandwidth, memory capacity, driver versions and hardware health.

first_principles.problem: A training job runs at 30% GPU utilisation, and engineers assume the model code is the bottleneck.

analogy.title: A specialised factory next door
analogy.story: Your office (CPU) sends raw materials by truck (PCIe) to a huge factory (GPU); if trucks are slow, the factory sits idle.
analogy.breaks: Factories store inventory; GPU memory is small relative to datasets.

example.title: Starved GPU
flow: Fix: more DataLoader workers, GPU decode

check.q: Why can a GPU show low utilisation even with heavy model code?
check.a: It may be waiting for data from the CPU (loading, preprocessing, transfers) rather than computing.

the-driver-stack-kernel-vs-user-space.core: The NVIDIA stack has kernel modules (nvidia.ko for core, nvidia-uvm for unified memory, nvidia-modeset and nvidia-drm) that manage hardware, memory mapping, interrupts and isolation, plus user-space libraries (libcuda.so, the driver API, the CUDA runtime, cuDNN, NCCL) that apps link against. The kernel driver and libcuda versions must match, and the CUDA toolkit version must be supported by the driver. Containers get the user-space libraries injected via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.

first_principles.problem: A container fails with 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version' after a node image update.
truths: Kernel and user parts must match.
CUDA runtime needs a minimum driver.
Containers share the host kernel driver.

analogy.title: A building's electrical system and plug-in appliances
analogy.story: The wiring (kernel driver) must match the voltage appliances (CUDA libraries) expect.
analogy.breaks: Appliances can use adapters; CUDA versions must genuinely be compatible.

code.text:
nvidia-smi | head -4         # Driver Version: 550.90.07  CUDA Version: 12.4
cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version
python -c 'import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)'   # 12.6 > 12.4 → mismatch
# fix: upgrade driver or use image built for CUDA ≤ 12.4

check.q: What does the 'CUDA Version' in nvidia-smi output mean?
check.a: The maximum CUDA runtime version the installed driver supports, not the toolkit installed.

pcie-topology-and-numa-affinity.core: GPUs connect via PCIe lanes to a specific CPU socket's root complex, sometimes through PCIe switches. On multi-socket servers, a process on socket 0 using a GPU attached to socket 1 must cross the inter-socket link (UPI/Infinity Fabric) for every transfer, adding latency and reducing bandwidth. Bind processes and memory to the GPU's NUMA node, and pair GPUs with the NICs on the same switch for RDMA.

first_principles.problem: Two identical GPUs on the same server show 30% different data-loading throughput.
derivation: Pair **GPU and NIC** on same switch.

analogy.title: Offices on two floors sharing one lift
analogy.story: Staff on floor 1 using a printer on floor 2 wait for the lift every time.
analogy.breaks: Lifts are visible; NUMA penalties hide in throughput numbers.

code.text:
nvidia-smi topo -m          # CPU Affinity / NUMA Affinity columns
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:81:00.0/numa_node   # 1
numactl --cpunodebind=1 --membind=1 python train.py --gpu 1
lspci -vv -s 81:00.0 | grep -E 'LnkSta:'          # Speed 16GT/s, Width x16

check.q: Why bind a GPU workload's CPU threads to the GPU's NUMA node?
check.a: To avoid cross-socket transfers over the interconnect, reducing latency and increasing host-device bandwidth.

nvlink-vs-pcie-for-multi-gpu-communicati.core: Multi-GPU training exchanges gradients constantly through all-reduce. Over PCIe (about 64 GB/s for Gen5 x16, often via the CPU or a switch) that becomes a bottleneck. NVLink and NVSwitch connect GPUs directly with far higher bandwidth (hundreds of GB/s to over 900 GB/s per GPU) and lower latency, enabling efficient tensor and data parallelism. NCCL automatically picks the fastest path, so topology determines scaling efficiency.

first_principles.problem: Training scales from 1 to 4 GPUs well but barely improves from 4 to 8 on a PCIe-only server.
truths: Gradient sync scales with GPU count.

analogy.title: Teams sharing notes by courier vs a direct hotline
analogy.story: Couriers (PCIe via CPU) are slow; a dedicated hotline (NVLink) lets teams sync instantly.
analogy.breaks: Hotlines are point-to-point; NVSwitch gives all-to-all.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Explains poor scaling on PCIe servers.

code.text:
nvidia-smi topo -m      # NV12 between GPUs = NVLink; PHB/SYS = PCIe paths
./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8M -e 1G -f 2 -g 8
# busbw: NVSwitch ~400 GB/s vs PCIe ~20 GB/s

check.q: What do 'SYS' and 'NV#' mean in nvidia-smi topo -m output?
check.a: SYS means traffic crosses the inter-socket link (slow PCIe path); NV# means direct NVLink connections.

gpudirect-rdma-bypassing-the-cpu-entirel.core: Normally, sending GPU data over the network copies GPU memory to host RAM, then the NIC reads host RAM. GPUDirect RDMA lets RDMA-capable NICs (InfiniBand or RoCE) read and write GPU memory directly over PCIe, bypassing host memory and CPU copies. Combined with NCCL, it's essential for multi-node training at scale, but it needs the GPU and NIC under the same PCIe switch, the right kernel modules (nvidia-peermem) and an RDMA fabric.

first_principles.problem: Multi-node training is limited by CPU memory copies for every gradient exchange.
truths: Copies through host memory add latency.
NICs can DMA to any PCIe device.
derivation: Place **GPU and NIC under same switch**.

analogy.title: Loading cargo directly from ship to train
analogy.story: Instead of unloading to a warehouse first, the crane moves containers straight across.
analogy.breaks: Cranes work anywhere on the dock; RDMA needs PCIe proximity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: GPU-to-GPU across nodes without host copies.

code.text:
lsmod | grep nvidia_peermem
export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5 NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=PHB
torchrun --nnodes 4 --nproc-per-node 8 train.py 2>&1 | grep -i 'GDRDMA'
# NCCL INFO Channel 00/0 : 0[0] -> 8[0] [send] via NET/IB/0/GDRDMA

check.q: What kernel module enables GPUDirect RDMA with NVIDIA GPUs and Mellanox NICs?

unified-memory-and-gpu-page-faults.core: CUDA Unified Memory (cudaMallocManaged) gives one pointer valid on both CPU and GPU. The nvidia-uvm driver migrates pages on demand: when the GPU touches a page that lives in host memory, a GPU page fault triggers migration. That simplifies code and allows oversubscribing GPU memory, but fault-driven migration can be far slower than explicit bulk copies, so use prefetching (cudaMemPrefetchAsync) and memory hints.

first_principles.problem: A port to unified memory runs 5× slower due to thousands of page faults per iteration.

analogy.title: A shared library book that moves on request
analogy.story: Whoever needs it gets it delivered, but constant back-and-forth requests waste time; better to deliver it in advance.
analogy.breaks: Books move one at a time; pages migrate in chunks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Faults eliminated; speed back to explicit-copy level.

check.q: Why can unified memory be slower than explicit cudaMemcpy?
check.a: Pages migrate on demand via GPU page faults, each with overhead, instead of efficient bulk transfers.

debugging-with-nvidia-smi-basic-monitori.core: nvidia-smi is the first tool. It shows per-GPU utilisation (the fraction of time a kernel was running, not how many cores were busy), memory used and total, temperature, power draw against cap, clocks, processes with their memory, ECC errors and persistence mode. Use nvidia-smi dmon or --query-gpu with --format=csv -l 1 for time series, and DCGM exporter for Prometheus. Low utilisation with full memory often means data starvation.

first_principles.problem: GPUs show 100% 'utilisation', yet training is slow, because utilisation only means a kernel was running.
truths: Power and clocks reveal real load.

analogy.title: A car's dashboard
analogy.story: 'Engine running' (utilisation) doesn't mean full throttle; RPM and fuel use (power, clocks) tell the real story.
analogy.breaks: Cars have one engine; GPUs have many SMs with varying activity.

branches.label: Caveat
children: Util = time busy, not SM occupancy

code.text:
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,memory.used,power.draw,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm --format=csv -l 1
nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE | grep -A10 'Clocks Event Reasons'
#   SW Power Cap : Active   ← throttled by power limit

check.q: Why can GPU-Util be 100% while performance is poor?
check.a: It only shows a kernel was running during the sample; kernels may use few SMs or be throttled by power or thermals.

debugging-with-nvidia-smi-topology-and-a.core: nvidia-smi topo -m prints the connection matrix between GPUs and NICs. NV# means NVLink with that many links; PIX means the same PCIe switch; PXB means multiple switches; PHB means through the CPU host bridge; NODE means same NUMA node across bridges; SYS means across sockets (slowest). It also lists CPU and NUMA affinity per GPU. Use it to place processes, choose GPU pairs for jobs and diagnose slow NCCL rings.

first_principles.problem: A 2-GPU job gets GPUs 0 and 5, which communicate across sockets, and runs slowly.
truths: Not all GPU pairs are equal.

analogy.title: A building's corridor map
analogy.story: Some offices are next door, others across the courtyard; seat collaborating teams close together.
analogy.breaks: Corridors don't change; topology differs per server model.

branches.label: Best→worst
children: NV# > PIX > PXB > PHB > NODE > SYS

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Job runs 2× faster than on GPUs 0+5.

code.text:
nvidia-smi topo -m
#        GPU0  GPU1  GPU5  mlx5_0  CPU Affinity  NUMA
# GPU0    X    NV12  SYS   PIX     0-31          0
# GPU1   NV12   X    SYS   PIX     0-31          0
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 numactl -N 0 python train.py   # NVLink pair, local NUMA, local NIC

check.q: Which topology code indicates the slowest GPU-to-GPU path?
check.a: SYS, meaning traffic crosses the inter-socket interconnect.

xid-errors-when-hardware-fails.core: Xid messages are NVIDIA driver error reports in the kernel log (dmesg or journal: 'NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00): 79...'). Each code indicates a class: 13 and 31 are usually application faults (illegal memory access, page fault); 43 means the GPU stopped processing; 48 and 63/64 relate to ECC errors and row remapping; 74 is NVLink errors; 79 means the GPU fell off the bus (hardware, power or thermal); 92 and 94/95 are ECC errors. Map codes to actions: fix code, reset the GPU, drain the node or RMA.

first_principles.problem: Training jobs crash randomly on one node, and nobody checks the kernel log.
truths: Codes distinguish app bugs from hardware.

analogy.title: Engine warning codes
analogy.story: Some codes mean 'you put in the wrong fuel' (app bug), others 'the engine block is cracked' (hardware).
analogy.breaks: Car codes are standardised across makes; Xid codes are NVIDIA-specific.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bad GPU removed; jobs stop crashing.

code.text:
journalctl -k | grep -i 'NVRM: Xid' | tail
# NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus.
nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,ROW_REMAPPER | grep -E 'Pending|Uncorr'
kubectl drain gpu-node-12 --ignore-daemonsets   # hardware issue → drain + RMA

check.a: The GPU has fallen off the PCIe bus, usually a hardware, power or thermal problem requiring node drain and investigation.
